clue.text: Asiatic with a sound connection

indicators.note: with a sound tells us the next word is to be heard rather than read, giving a soundalike

parts.note: a tie is a link or connection

explanation.surface: Someone from Asia is linked to something audible, perhaps a telephone line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with a sound' signals that TIE, a connection, is said aloud and gives a word that sounds the same, the Asian nationality.
explanation.definitionFit: A person from Thailand is an Asian, so the nationality noun fits the broader word Asiatic.

clue.text: Is breaking the record, so to speak

indicators.note: breaking into means one piece forces its way inside another

parts.note: LP is a long-playing record
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone smashes a record, or at least that is the figure of speech.
explanation.walkthrough: 'record' suggests a sporting best, but it is the vinyl kind. The definition is loose: a lisp is one particular way of talking, which 'so to speak' points at.
explanation.definitionFit: A lisp is a speech impediment, a manner of pronouncing sibilants, so it is one way to speak.

clue.text: Master of Arts before the revolution

indicators.note: a revolution turns things over, so the letters of Arts are turned into a new order

explanation.surface: A university degree held by someone in the years before an uprising.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Master of Arts' looks like the MA degree, but 'Master' alone is the definition and 'the revolution' rearranges ARTS. The Russian ruler was overthrown in the 1917 revolution, so the surface fits the answer too.
explanation.definitionFit: The Russian emperor was the supreme ruler, the absolute lord and master of his subjects.

clue.text: Vessel can hold something fit to drink

parts.note: a pot is a cooking or drinking vessel
to be able is to be capable, so can means able

explanation.surface: A container is said to be capable of holding a drinkable liquid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hold' is a link here; the definition is a noun, since a potable is a drinkable liquid.
explanation.definitionFit: Used as a noun, a potable is any beverage safe and suitable for drinking.

clue.text: Observe noted small gems

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held, 'Observe noted small gems', parses as SEE (observe) + D (a note) + PEARLS (gems), but 'gems' is then also needed in the definition 'small gems'; no word is left to give PEARLS separately, so one word does two jobs.

clue.text: Hardware shop 66 long?

parts.note: a surveyor's measure of sixty-six feet shares its name with a run of linked metal rings, so a hardware shop could stock that length; read the other way it is a retail business with many branches

explanation.surface: A question about the length of an ironmonger's premises.
explanation.walkthrough: A chain is an old British surveying length of 22 yards, that is 66 feet; a shop selling chains would be a chain store, which really means one of many branches under one owner.
explanation.definitionFit: A retail outlet that belongs to a group of identical branches is the ordinary sense; the clue imagines a shop selling metal links.

clue.text: First class questionnaire?

parts.note: an entry is the first coming in, an admission or beginning
in British schools a form is a class of pupils

explanation.surface: A top-quality survey, or a survey of the best pupils.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First class' reads as excellent, but splits into two nouns: a first coming in and the British school word for a class of pupils. The question mark admits that an application document is only loosely a questionnaire.
explanation.definitionFit: An application document asks the applicant a series of questions, so it is a kind of survey sheet.

clue.text: In Wales she doesn't take tea, one hears

indicators.note: doesn't take means a letter is left out of the word before it

parts.note: Gwent is a former county in south-east Wales
tea spoken aloud is the letter T

explanation.surface: A Welsh woman who declines a cup of tea, according to rumour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In Wales' stands for GWENT, an old Welsh county; 'doesn't take' drops the T that 'tea, one hears' sounds like, leaving a Welsh woman's name.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman's given name, common in Wales, stands in for the pronoun she.

clue.text: Red-head that takes the biscuit

definitions.meaning: a person with red hair is nicknamed ginger, and the head is jokingly a nut

explanation.definitionFit: A ginger-haired person's head is slangily a nut, and the same words name a hard spiced British biscuit.

clue.text: Significant I'm left on board with a busybody

parts.note: taken as written, without its apostrophe
port is the left-hand side of a ship
the ant is proverbially busy, always at work

explanation.surface: Someone claims to matter, being on the left aboard ship beside a meddler.
explanation.walkthrough: 'busybody' is not a meddler here but a busy body, the hard-working ANT; 'left on board' is PORT, the left of a ship.
explanation.definitionFit: Something weighty, of real consequence, is significant.

clue.text: Round to start a fight

parts.note: the opening round of a boxing bout is given its number; the clue describes that number

explanation.surface: A boxer calls for a first bout to get going.
explanation.walkthrough: Boxing matches are fought in numbered rounds, and the first is 'round one', so the number is the round that starts the fight.
explanation.definitionFit: A bout's first round is numbered as the single unit, the first number counted.

clue.text: Possibly no degree (second) for one who does this

definitions.text: Possibly no degree (second) for one who does this

parts.note: taken as written
D is short for degree, as in a qualification

explanation.surface: A student who keeps dozing off may leave without a degree, not even a second.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition too: someone who keeps dropping off in lectures may get no degree, not even a second-class one.
explanation.definitionFit: Dozing off, the head drops forward, and a sleepy student who does it may well fail.

clue.text: Fit for tackling

definitions.meaning: to fit out or equip, as a ship is fitted out
a ship's tackle, its ropes and gear

explanation.definitionFit: To equip a vessel is to rig it, and its rigging is its tackle of ropes and spars.

clue.text: Actually sounds rubbish to a friend

indicators.note: sounds tells us the words are heard aloud and give a soundalike

parts.note: litter is rubbish and an ally is a friend

explanation.surface: A remark that truly sounds like nonsense addressed to a mate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sounds' signals that LITTER (rubbish) plus ALLY (friend), said aloud, gives the answer; 'to a' joins them.
explanation.definitionFit: Literally means in fact, really, without exaggeration, so it can replace actually.

clue.text: Profligate maybe, but at least he's not tight

definitions.meaning: a dissolute person who lives immorally
a liver that is loose is not tight, with tight also suggesting drunk or stingy

explanation.definitionFit: A dissolute person leads a slack, immoral life, while the second reading is a body organ described as slack.

clue.text: Appropriate girl to be offended by

parts.note: to appropriate something is to take it
a miss is a girl or young woman, with A from the clue's implied article

explanation.surface: Seize a young woman and she will be upset by it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Appropriate' looks like an adjective meaning suitable, but it is the verb meaning seize. 'girl' gives A MISS.
explanation.definitionFit: To resent a remark or feel hurt by it is to receive it wrongly, the idiom meaning to be offended by.

clue.text: Giving up plaster-work

definitions.meaning: to render up is to surrender or hand over
a coat of plaster or cement on an outside wall

explanation.definitionFit: Handing over is one sense of the verb; the noun is a builder's coat of plaster on a wall.

clue.text: Expenses writers forgo for unknown quantities

indicators.note: forgo means do without, so a group of letters is removed from the word

parts.note: pens are instruments for writing

explanation.surface: Writers give up their claim to expenses in exchange for something uncertain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'writers' are PENS, not authors; 'forgo' takes them out of EXPENSES. In algebra an unknown quantity is written x, so several are 'xs'.
explanation.definitionFit: Mathematicians write an unknown as the letter x, so a number of unknowns are that letter in the plural.

clue.text: Doing sovereign work on the soil?

definitions.text: Doing sovereign work on the soil?

parts.words: Doing sovereign work on the soil?
parts.note: working on behalf of a monarch splits as 'for' plus a ruler, while digging soil with a garden implement is the everyday sense

explanation.surface: A gardener toils in the earth on behalf of the monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: Split in two the answer reads 'for king', serving the sovereign; as one word it means turning soil with a garden fork.
explanation.definitionFit: Breaking up soil with a pronged garden tool is the gardening sense; the split reading is serving a monarch.

clue.text: It isn't rural in the broadest sense

definitions.text: It isn't rural in the broadest sense

parts.words: It isn't rural in the broadest sense
parts.note: the word for open land outside towns, taken in its widest meaning, names a whole nation including its cities

explanation.surface: A remark that, taken broadly, a place is not really the countryside.
explanation.walkthrough: The word means rural land as opposed to town, but in its broadest sense it is a whole nation, cities and all, so then it is not rural.
explanation.definitionFit: A nation or state is the broad meaning, and a nation takes in its towns as well as farmland.

clue.text: Assign a place for commuters, say

definitions.meaning: to post someone to a particular spot
a stop on a railway line where travellers board trains

explanation.definitionFit: To post a soldier somewhere is the verb; the noun is the railway stop where commuters board.

clue.text: Our last letter to the Greeks

definitions.text: Our last letter to the Greeks

parts.words: Our last letter to the Greeks
parts.note: the final letter of the English alphabet, as the Greek alphabet names it

explanation.surface: A final message written to the people of Greece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'letter' suggests correspondence, but it is an alphabet letter: the English z corresponds to the sixth Greek letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek character corresponding to the English z is its sixth letter.

clue.text: Reckons one million is sunk in landed property

indicators.note: is sunk in means placed inside, as money is sunk into property

parts.note: estates are areas of land owned by one person
the Roman numeral for one is I

explanation.surface: An investor calculates that a fortune has been invested in land.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is sunk in' reads as investing, but puts I and M inside ESTATES.
explanation.definitionFit: To estimate is to calculate roughly, so estimates and reckons are synonyms.

clue.text: A British airborne visitor

parts.note: UK stands for the United Kingdom, so British

explanation.surface: A traveller from Britain arriving by plane.
explanation.walkthrough: 'airborne visitor' suggests a passenger flight, but it is a seabird that visits coasts.
explanation.definitionFit: A diving seabird of northern coasts, it flies in from the sea, so a winged guest.

clue.text: Spoil my first afternoon with the king

indicators.note: first takes the opening letter of each of the two words around it

parts.note: R is short for rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: Someone complains that the monarch ruined their first afternoon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'first' sits between 'my' and 'afternoon' and takes the first letter of each, M and A; R is Rex, king.
explanation.definitionFit: To spoil something is to damage or blemish it.

clue.text: Where to return if James head is cut in two

indicators.note: to return means to go back, so the little word is read backwards
head means the first letter of the name
cut in two halves the short word, keeping its front half

explanation.surface: A destination to go back to if a man named James suffers a split head.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to return' turns IF into FI; 'head' takes J from James; 'cut in two' halves 'is' to I. 'Where' alone is the definition, a place.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is a place, an island nation in the Pacific, so it answers the question where.

clue.text: Tipped off perhaps, getting the wink on .

indicators.note: getting here means producing by rearranging, so the letters of the phrase are worked into new order

explanation.surface: Someone receives a knowing wink as a signal, leading into the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'getting' signals an anagram of THE WINK ON. The ellipsis carries on into 29-across.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone tipped off has inside information, so is well informed.

clue.text: Key study of the original garden

parts.note: E is a musical key
a den is a private study or room

explanation.surface: A crucial study of the first garden in the Bible.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Key' looks like important, but is the musical key E; DEN is a study.
explanation.definitionFit: In Genesis the first garden, where Adam and Eve lived, is the biblical paradise.

clue.text: Want to change 26

indicators.note: to change means to alter, so the letters of the other answer are rearranged

parts.note: 26 refers to the answer of 26-down, the garden

explanation.surface: A desire to alter a cross-reference.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to change' rearranges the letters of the answer to 26-down.
explanation.definitionFit: A lack or requirement is a want, the noun or verb sense of needing something.

clue.text: Where it's said, to look for a really big bed

definitions.text: to look for a really big bed

indicators.note: it's said tells us the word is heard aloud, giving a soundalike

parts.note: taken as written, and said aloud

explanation.surface: A question about where to go to find an enormous bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Where', said aloud, gives the answer. Ware is a town in Hertfordshire, England, home of the Great Bed of Ware, an enormous Elizabethan bed now in the Victoria and Albert Museum.
explanation.definitionFit: The Hertfordshire town gave its name to a famous giant bed, so it is the place to find it.

clue.text: … certain items from all quarters

definitions.meaning: reports or bulletins of recent events
the four compass points north, east, west and south

explanation.definitionFit: Reports are broadcast items, and the four points of the compass are the quarters, with initials making the word.

clue.text: Third party fruit

definitions.meaning: an unwanted extra person with a courting couple

explanation.definitionFit: An unwanted chaperone tagging along with lovers is the British idiom; the other is a sharp green berry.
